The Heirloom Promise

Four guarantees, every object, every release.

Every object sold under the Heirloom imprint is released with the same four undertakings. The trade-back, in particular, is non-negotiable. It is the mechanic that proves the thesis.

01 · Provenance

A documented history.

Origin, period, material, and prior life where known. Plainly stated, not romanticised.

02 · Condition

An honest statement.

Including imperfection. Patina, paint loss, surface rust, repair — all described as found. Nothing softened.

03 · Custodianship

A note on living with it.

How to place it, how to maintain it, what to expect from the material over the next decade of weather.

04 · Trade-back

A lifetime offer.

We will buy any object back into the catalogue at fair market value. Always. Transferable to the next steward.

Patina is provenance.

Concrete takes on lichen and the soft green of moss. Cement crazes to a fine map of cracks. Iron rises to a warm rust bloom. Each surface holds the record of a life already lived, and none of it has been corrected.

On material

Concrete leads, because concrete survived.

The dominant material of mid-twentieth century garden manufacture — urns, troughs, birdbaths, balustrades, the entire post-war suburban garden — was cast concrete. It is heavy, weathers honestly, and develops a patina that no other material matches.

We collect concrete first. Terracotta, stone, iron, timber, glass follow.

On wear

Imperfection is the evidence.

Paint loss, surface rust, edge wear, lichen colonies, crazed glazes — these are not flaws. They are the documentation of the object having been used in a real garden, in real weather, for a real length of time.

We do not erase them. We describe them.

On the trade-back

Custodianship is finite. The object is not.

You are not buying an object. You are taking custody of one. When the time comes to release it — when the garden changes, when the steward changes, when the object is ready for its next decade — we will buy it back into the catalogue.

Lifetime. Transferable. Plainly stated.

"We do not sell decor. We sell custodianship."
On the imprint

Heirloom is a curatorial imprint, not a shop.

An imprint, in the publishing sense: a specialised label within a parent house, with its own voice and its own catalogue. Heirloom relates to Gardener & Son the way a publishing imprint relates to its publisher — distinct register, shared spine.

"Kept, not bought."

We acquire vintage garden objects of material truth — cast concrete, cement, stone, iron, copper, timber, glass — and re-release them with full provenance and a standing offer of trade-back. The catalogue is small by design. We say no more than we say yes.

This is not nostalgia. The objects in this catalogue have already proven their durability. They were kept once. They are worth keeping again.

By material

The catalogue, organised.

Concrete

The lead material. Urns, troughs, birdbaths, figurative pieces.

Cement

Finer cast pieces — figurative birds, smaller vessels, decorative work.

Stone

Bluestone, basalt, sandstone. Single-piece pieces. Generational.

Iron

Cast and wrought. Urns, gates, hand tools, finials.

Released from the studio of Gardener & Son.

An ecological design practice working across Melbourne and the Otway region. The studio designs gardens built to last; Heirloom is the parallel discipline of finding the objects that belong in them. One unified ecological culture, two registers.

Heirloom is a Gardener & Son imprint. We acknowledge the Traditional Custodians of the land on which we work and live — the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung people of the Kulin Nation — and pay our respects to their Elders past and present. We recognise that this land was never ceded and that the deep knowledge of Country held by its First Peoples is the longest and most enduring record of how to live well within it.

Cast concrete · Steel legs · Australian · c. 1950–1970

Mid-Century Cast Concrete Garden Stork.

Status
Released
Origin

Australian

Acquired from a private garden in regional Victoria.

Period

c. 1950–1970

Cast in the post-war Australian decorative concrete tradition.

Material

Concrete & steel

Cast concrete body and base, two slender steel legs.

Condition

Weathered

Structurally sound, original paint, surface rust to legs.

A life-sized garden stork in cast concrete, hand-painted and weathered by decades outdoors. The body holds its original paint — chalked and crazed to a soft white, the wing picked out in charcoal grey — and stands on two slender steel legs set into a cast concrete base moulded as a shallow plinth.

The construction is the period speaking plainly: concrete for the body and base, where mass and weather-resistance mattered, and steel for the legs, where concrete could never have held the span. It is why the stork is still standing. Most of its contemporaries are not.

The wear is the record. Paint loss across the breast and back, surface crazing along the neck, a warm rust bloom rising up both legs where the steel has done its honest work, and the soft green-grey bloom that only arrives on concrete left in real weather. Nothing here has been corrected.

Figural garden birds of this period — storks, herons, cranes, flamingos — were cast to bring a note of theatre to mid-century suburban gardens. Most were used hard and discarded. This one was kept.

OriginAustralian

Cast cement · Hand-painted · Australian · c. 1950–1970

Mid-Century Cast Cement Garden Duck.

Status
Released
Origin

Australian

Acquired from a regional garden, NSW.

Period

c. 1950–1970

Made in number for mid-century Australian gardens.

Material

Cast cement

Fine cement mix. Crisply moulded feathering and base.

Condition

Weathered

Structurally sound. Original hand-painting, ochre bill intact.

A garden duck in cast cement, modelled standing with the neck raised and the bill lifted slightly skyward. The casting is a good one — the wing and breast feathering is crisply defined, the form generous and well-proportioned — and it sits on an integral base moulded to suggest a low mound of reeds.

It holds its original hand-painting: a soft chalked white across the body, the bill picked out in warm ochre. Decades outdoors have crazed the paint to a fine map of cracks and worn it back in places to the pale cement beneath. The wear is even, unforced, and entirely the record of a life spent in a real garden.

Cast cement waterfowl were a fixture of mid-century Australian gardens — set at pond edges, in rockeries, beside birdbaths. They were made in number and most were used until they broke or were cleared away. This one was kept, and it is sound.

Bluestone · c. 1960s · Central Victoria

1960s Bluestone Garden Birdbath.

Status
Released
Origin

Central Victoria

Quarried near Castlemaine.

Period

c. 1960s

Made for a garden in Kew. Acquired from the estate.

Material

Bluestone

Single-piece basalt, hand-cut and ground.

Condition

Weathered

Lichen colonies, edge wear from six decades of weather.

A bluestone birdbath cut from a single piece of basalt and ground shallow across its face. Sixty years of weather have softened the original tool marks and established lichen and moss colonies in the sheltered margins of the bowl.

It holds standing water. Over time, leaf fall and algae gather at the margins. This is the surface becoming part of the garden's biology, not deterioration.

Bluestone is generational material. It will be in a garden long after most other things have moved on.
